Content:
Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|6; 0|3]] Given that [MATH: \lambda=3] is an eigenvalue of [MATH: A,] how can we find an eigenvector that corresponds to this eigenvalue?

Content:
Recall that a non-zero vector [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] with corresponding eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] if

Content:
[MATH: A{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}={\color{red}\lambda}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.]

Content:
We can rewrite this equation, substituting [MATH: {\color{red}{\lambda = 3}},] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Av|= 3v; Av − 3v|= 0; Av − 3Iv|= 0; (A − 3I)v|= 0]

Content:
So, to find an eigenvector of [MATH: A] that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda = {\color{red}3},] we need to find a non-zero solution of the equation

Content:
[MATH: (A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: A − 3I|= [2|6; 0|3] − 3[1|0; 0|1]; = [− 1|6; 0|0].]

Content:
Therefore, the equation [MATH: (A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}] corresponds to the following homogeneous system of linear equations:

Content:
[MATH: {− x_{1} + 6x_{2} = 0; 0 = 0.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: A-{\color{red}3}I] is already in row echelon form, and it has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. Moreover, from the first equation, we get [MATH: x_1=6x_2,] which implies that the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: [6x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Content:
We only require one eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda={\color{red}3}.] Setting [MATH: x_2=1,] we obtain the eigenvector

Content:
[MATH: [6; 1]]

Content:
Note: If we set [MATH: x_2=2,] we'll get a different eigenvector, namely
[MATH: [12; 2]]
Note that [MATH: \mathbf w] is also an eigenvector that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda=3.] In fact, we can choose any real [MATH: x_2 \neq 0] to generate an eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = 3.]

Content:
Watch out! In the case of [MATH: x_2=0,] we get the zero vector, but this is not an eigenvector. Remember that eigenvectors must be non-zero vectors.

sections.normalized_html: If [MATH: [a; b]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [2|5; − 1|− 4]] that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \,\lambda=1], then what is the value of [MATH: \,\dfrac{b}{a}\,?]
sections.readable_text:
If [MATH: [a; b]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [2|5; − 1|− 4]]
that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \,\lambda=1], then what is the value of [MATH: \,\dfrac{b}{a}\,?]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation [MATH: (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: \,\lambda =1.] So, we have

[MATH: A − λI|= [2|5; − 1|− 4] − [1|0; 0|1]; = [1|5; − 1|− 5].]

We have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations: [MATH: {x_{1} + 5x_{2} = 0; − x_{1} − 5x_{2} = 0]

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [1|5|0; − 1|− 5|0]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + R_{1}; ∼[1|5|0; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable.

From the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: x_1+5x_2=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=-5x_2.]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: [− 5x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Setting, for instance, [MATH: x_2=-1,] we get the following eigenvector:

[MATH: [a; b]]

Finally, [MATH: \dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{-1}{5}=-\dfrac{1}{5}.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation [MATH: (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: \,\lambda =2.] So, we get

[MATH: A − λI|= [7|− 4; 5|− 2] − 2[1|0; 0|1]; = [5|− 4; 5|− 4].]

We have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations: [MATH: {5x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 0; 5x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 0]

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [5|− 4|0; 5|− 4|0]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[5|− 4|0; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable.

From the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: 5x_1-4x_2=0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad x_1=\dfrac{4}{5}x_2.]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: [(4)/(5)x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Finally, setting [MATH: x_2=5,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [4; 5]]

items.title: Finding Two Linearly Independent Eigenvectors of a 2x2 Matrix

sections.normalized_html: Given that [MATH: \lambda=1] and [MATH: \lambda=-4] are the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: [1|− 1; 0|− 4]] find two linearly independent eigenvectors of [MATH: A.]
sections.readable_text:
Given that [MATH: \lambda=1] and [MATH: \lambda=-4] are the eigenvalues of the matrix
[MATH: [1|− 1; 0|− 4]]
find two linearly independent eigenvectors of [MATH: A.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
We can get two linearly independent eigenvectors by simply finding eigenvectors corresponding to the different eigenvalues.

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation

[MATH: (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

With that in mind, let's consider each of the eigenvalues separately.

  • For [MATH: \lambda =1,] we have [MATH: A − λI|= [1|− 1; 0|− 4] − 1[1|0; 0|1]; = [0|− 1; 0|− 5].] We have to solve the corresponding system of linear equations: [MATH: {− x_{2} = 0; − 5x_{2} = 0] So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows: [MATH: M|= [0|− 1|0; 0|− 5|0]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 5)R_{1}; ∼[0|− 1|0; 0|0|0]] In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the [MATH: 2]nd one). lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Consider the matrix [MATH: [2|6; 0|3]] Given that [MATH: \lambda=3] is an eigenvalue of [MATH: A,] how can we find an eigenvector that corresponds to this eigenvalue?

Content:
Recall that a non-zero vector [MATH: \color{blue}\mathbf{v}] is an eigenvector of [MATH: A] with corresponding eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] if

Content:
[MATH: A{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}={\color{red}\lambda}{\color{blue}\mathbf{v}}.]

Content:
We can rewrite this equation, substituting [MATH: {\color{red}{\lambda = 3}},] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: Av|= 3v; Av − 3v|= 0; Av − 3Iv|= 0; (A − 3I)v|= 0]

Content:
So, to find an eigenvector of [MATH: A] that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda = {\color{red}3},] we need to find a non-zero solution of the equation

Content:
[MATH: (A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}.]

Content:
In our case, we have

Content:
[MATH: A − 3I|= [2|6; 0|3] − 3[1|0; 0|1]; = [− 1|6; 0|0].]

Content:
Therefore, the equation [MATH: (A- {\color{red}3} I){\color{blue}\mathbf{v}} = \mathbf{0}] corresponds to the following homogeneous system of linear equations:

Content:
[MATH: {− x_{1} + 6x_{2} = 0; 0 = 0.]

Content:
Notice that [MATH: A-{\color{red}3}I] is already in row echelon form, and it has one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable. Moreover, from the first equation, we get [MATH: x_1=6x_2,] which implies that the general solution is

Content:
[MATH: [6x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Content:
We only require one eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda={\color{red}3}.] Setting [MATH: x_2=1,] we obtain the eigenvector

Content:
[MATH: [6; 1]]

Content:
Note: If we set [MATH: x_2=2,] we'll get a different eigenvector, namely
[MATH: [12; 2]]
Note that [MATH: \mathbf w] is also an eigenvector that corresponds to [MATH: \lambda=3.] In fact, we can choose any real [MATH: x_2 \neq 0] to generate an eigenvector corresponding to [MATH: \lambda = 3.]

Content:
Watch out! In the case of [MATH: x_2=0,] we get the zero vector, but this is not an eigenvector. Remember that eigenvectors must be non-zero vectors.

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Components of an Eigenvector Corresponding to an Eigenvalue

Example Prompt:
If [MATH: [a; b]] is an eigenvector of [MATH: [2|5; − 1|− 4]]
that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \,\lambda=1], then what is the value of [MATH: \,\dfrac{b}{a}\,?]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation
[MATH: (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: \,\lambda =1.] So, we have

[MATH: A − λI|= [2|5; − 1|− 4] − [1|0; 0|1]; = [1|5; − 1|− 5].]

We have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:
[MATH: {x_{1} + 5x_{2} = 0; − x_{1} − 5x_{2} = 0]

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [1|5|0; − 1|− 5|0]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + R_{1}; ∼[1|5|0; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable.

From the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: x_1+5x_2=0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=-5x_2.]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: [− 5x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Setting, for instance, [MATH: x_2=-1,] we get the following eigenvector:

[MATH: [a; b]]

Finally, [MATH: \dfrac{b}{a}=\dfrac{-1}{5}=-\dfrac{1}{5}.]

Item 5 — Example: Calculating an Eigenvector Corresponding to an Eigenvalue

Example Prompt:
Find an eigenvector of [MATH: [7|− 4; 5|− 2]]
that corresponds to the eigenvalue [MATH: \,\lambda=2.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation
[MATH: (A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.]

In our case, we have [MATH: \,\lambda =2.] So, we get

[MATH: A − λI|= [7|− 4; 5|− 2] − 2[1|0; 0|1]; = [5|− 4; 5|− 4].]

We have to solve the corresponding homogeneous system of linear equations:
[MATH: {5x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 0; 5x_{1} − 4x_{2} = 0]

So, we row-reduce the augmented matrix [MATH: M] to row echelon form using Gaussian elimination, as follows:

[MATH: M|= [5|− 4|0; 5|− 4|0]|R_{2}:=R_{2} + (− 1)R_{1}; ∼[5|− 4|0; 0|0|0]]

In the reduced matrix above, there is one pivot column (the [MATH: 1]st one). So, [MATH: x_2] is a free variable.

From the first equation, we obtain

[MATH: 5x_1-4x_2=0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
x_1=\dfrac{4}{5}x_2.]

Therefore, the general solution is

[MATH: [(4)/(5)x_{2}; x_{2}]]

Finally, setting [MATH: x_2=5,] we get the eigenvector

[MATH: [4; 5]]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Connection Between Eigenspaces and Null Spaces

Content:
Given a matrix [MATH: A] with an eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda], the eigenspace [MATH: V_\lambda] can be defined as the set of all possible eigenvectors corresponding to [MATH: \lambda] plus the vector [MATH: \mathbf{0}{:}]
[MATH: eigenvectors]

Content:
Note that the eigenspace consists of all (not only non-zero) solutions of the equation [MATH: (A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.] So, the eigenspace can also be viewed as the null space of the matrix [MATH: A-\lambda I,] as follows:
[MATH: V_{\color{red}\lambda} = \textrm{Null}(A - {\color{red}\lambda} I).]

Content:
We also have the following theorem:

Content:
> Eigenvectors that correspond to different eigenvalues are always linearly independent.

Content:
For example, the matrix

Content:
[MATH: [1|− 2; 3|− 4]]

Content:
has eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1=-2] and [MATH: \lambda_2=-1,] for which the corresponding eigenvectors are

Content:
[MATH: [2; 3]]

Content:
Here, [MATH: \mathbf{v}_1] and [MATH: \mathbf{v}_2] are linearly independent (they are not collinear).

Content:
Watch out! Eigenvectors that correspond to the same eigenvalue can be (and very often will be) linearly dependent. For example, the vectors

Content:
[MATH: [1; 1]]

Content:
are collinear eigenvectors of the matrix [MATH: A] above that correspond to [MATH: \lambda_2=-1.]
